proposals.impact: unblocks daily content pipeline, restores automated publishing
proposals.observation: The Daily Blog Post workflow has failed every run in the last 24 hours (failed at 2026-09-08T08:05:15Z). The content queue shows only 1 post queued against 47 published — meaning the pipeline that feeds new posts is broken, not just slow. With the Funnel-Hack Digest also failing, two of three automated content workflows are down simultaneously. Joel has one post queued and a silent CI. If that queued post doesn't ship on schedule, the content calendar stalls entirely.
proposals.proposal:
Open the Daily Blog Post workflow file and read the failure logs to find what broke at 08:05 on 8 September. Common causes in Astro + GitHub Actions setups: a Node version mismatch after a package-lock update (the commit history shows package.json is on the blocked list, meaning a dependency may have drifted), an expired API key for the content-generation step, or a changed output path. Fix the specific failing step. Do not touch .github/workflows/* beyond this one file — and note that the safety rules block that path, so Joel must action this manually rather than Fred shipping it. Fred's role here is to flag it as the highest-priority item and supply the diagnostic path so Joel can open the correct file immediately.

Concrete next step: run `gh run view --log-failed` on the most recent Daily Blog Post run ID. The exit code and line number in the log will point to the broken step in under two minutes.

proposals.impact: reduces intro-to-q1 drop-off, increases quiz starts
proposals.observation: In the 48-hour quiz window, 3 sessions loaded the quiz page. 2 stopped at intro_load — they saw the intro screen and left without pressing start. Only 1 reached q1_shown, and that person did not complete. Completion rate is 0%. The intro screen is doing the most damage: it is losing two out of three visitors before a single question appears. The sources show 2 direct visits and 1 referral from the shop, which means people are arriving with intent — they typed the URL or clicked from a product page. The drop is not a traffic-quality problem; it is an intro-friction problem.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the quiz intro headline and sub-copy to remove any framing that asks visitors to commit to a "process" or "journey" before they know the payoff. The current text (placeholder shown below based on standard WoW quiz patterns — Joel should confirm verbatim copy) likely tells people what the quiz *is* rather than what they will *know* in 90 seconds. Replace it with a single concrete promise tied to the specific result: their money script, named. Keep the CTA button text short and outcome-led rather than process-led.
proposals.current_text: Discover your money personality and start your journey to financial clarity. This short quiz takes about 5 minutes to complete.
proposals.new_text: Most people earning good money still can't explain why they avoid the bank app, overspend after a stressful week, or save hard and then blow it. This quiz takes 90 seconds and names the pattern underneath.

proposals.impact: lifts 37.5% open rate closer to the 66% seen on Money Vigilance sequence
proposals.observation: The Money Worship automation has the lowest open rate in the sequence: 37.5% against Money Avoidance at 52.6% and Money Vigilance at 66.7%. All three sequences are live and sending to real subscribers, so this is not a sample-size artefact — 16 sends is a thin but directional number. The gap between Money Worship (37.5%) and Money Vigilance (66.7%) is 29 percentage points. The most likely cause is a subject line that either sounds like financial advice (triggering skip-past behaviour in people who already distrust finance content) or sounds generic enough that recipients don't see themselves in it. Money Worship subscribers are, by definition, people who tie their self-worth tightly to earning and status — they are the ICP cohort most likely to delete an email that sounds like it is lecturing them about money attitudes.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the subject line of the first Money Worship automation email to speak to the specific tension a Money Worship person feels on a Sunday evening — not their "relationship with money" in the abstract, but the concrete loop: earned more this month, still not enough, not sure why. The subject line should feel like Joel is inside their head, not outside looking in with a clipboard. Keep it under 50 characters so it renders fully on mobile without truncation.
proposals.current_text: Subject: Your money worship score — what it means for you
proposals.new_text: Subject: You earned more. It still didn't feel like enough.
